overview.title: Welcome to Go Sound 👋

sections.text: All the pages, in reading order

overview.text: Welcome to Go Sound 👋 Go Sound plays sound from Go programs : beeps, music, the sea, a foghorn. On phones, computers, web pages and the Nintendo 3DS. A program opens the speakers once, and plays as many sounds at once as it likes: notes it makes itself, or WAV and Ogg files it carries. Go Sound mixes them and sends them to each system's own audio. On a phone it goes quiet when the app leaves the screen. Is it for me? ✅ You write Go and want sound in a program, a game or a Go UI app. ✅ You want to understand what a sound is for a computer: samples, rates, mixing. Where to start Pick the line that sounds like you. If you… Read Time are new and want to hear something 🏴‍☠️ The quest : the sounds of a harbour, in 6 levels 40 min want to know how to use it in your program Using Go Sound 10 min have a sound file and wonder which format Sound files 5 min want to know why it is built this way The design — want to know what is coming Roadmap — All the pages, in reading order The menu on the left (or the files in docs/ ) follows this order. Start Overview : this page The quest : six levels, from a beep to an app Use Using Go Sound Sound files The project The design Roadmap 🚧 Not done yet The sound of films: Go Renderer decodes a film's pictures only (see the roadmap ). MP3 and Opus files. Android's audio focus: lowering the sound when another application plays. Heard on a phone and seen playing on the Android 14 emulator; a desktop and a browser are built for but not heard yet. Words you will meet Word What it means Go A programming language. To try these projects you install it once, from go.dev, and type go run … in a terminal. Terminal The window where you type commands: Terminal on macOS and Linux, PowerShell on Windows. Repository A project's folder of files, kept on GitHub. git clone <address> copies it to your computer. Quest The tutorial of these docs: short levels, each ending with something that works and an achievement. The family Go Sound is one of a family of small projects that work together: Project What it does Go Renderer draws 3D scenes and flat interfaces Go UI buttons, panels and whole applications Go UI for Android Android apps that look like Android's own Go Sound (this one) sound and music Go Scene Builder 3D scenes from a flat map Go Simulator simulations that change a scene Go Terrain Simulator ground shaped by rivers Go Climate Simulator weather and biomes Go Flora Simulator forests that grow Go Urban Simulator towns that grow Go Motion Simulator a scene that moves Go for 3DS Go on the Nintendo 3DS ⚠️ All of them are educational experiments , written with an AI assistant and pending review by their author: good for learning and playing, not for production.

roadmap.title: 🗺️ Roadmap
roadmap.text: 🗺️ Roadmap What is left, in the order it is best done. Phase 1 (this repository: a context, players, WAV and Ogg Vorbis, suspend and resume) is done, and was heard on a phone in October 2026. Phase 2: the sound of films A film's pictures play today (Go UI's window.Video ) and its sound does not. See the design for why it is split this way. Go Renderer ( android/video.c ): open the film's sound track with a second AMediaCodec ( audio/mp4a-latm for AAC, audio/opus ), from the same AMediaExtractor or a second one on the same file, and decode it a step at a time, as the pictures are. Hand out its samples (16-bit or float PCM, with the track's rate and channels from the output format) without playing them. Rewind and the film's end must reach the sound track too. Go UI ( window/video.go ): give the samples as a stream ( Read(samples []float32) , Format ), in a small interface of Go UI's own, so Go UI does not import Go Sound. Let Video take a clock ( func() time.Duration ) and show the picture due by then, dropping or repeating pictures; with no clock it keeps its own, as today. Joining them : a small package (here as sound/film , or in Go UI for Android) makes a Go Sound player of the film's stream and gives the film the player's Position as its clock. Play, pause and rewind go to both. In a browser : the film's <video> element plays its own sound in step with its pictures; unmute it after the person's first touch (it is muted now so it can start without one). Try it : the gallery's film ( cmd/gallery/coast.mp4 has no sound track yet: make one with ffmpeg), on the emulator and a phone, checking the pictures keep up with the sound. Phase 3: more Audio focus on Android : ask for it when a sound starts ( AudioManager.requestAudioFocus through JNI, in Go Renderer), lower or pause the sound when another application takes it. Volume by kind : music and effects turned up and down apart. MP3 and Opus : go-mp3 is archived; look at goxiph, kazzmir/opus-go and darui3018823/opus, and check them against reference files before choosing. A better resampler : linear interpolation is fine between 44.1 and 48 kHz; far apart rates (8 kHz speech) would sound cleaner through a short windowed filter. Hear the desktop and the web : both are built but not heard yet (the containers here have no sound device). A Go UI example with a button, run on a desktop and in a browser.

sound-files.title: 🎼 Sound files
sound-files.text: 🎼 Sound files Format Package Read WAV wav Integer samples of 8, 16, 24 and 32 bits, floating point ones of 32 and 64, any channels, any rate. Written here: a header and samples Ogg Vorbis vorbis Any Vorbis file, decoded in Go by jfreymuth/oggvorbis Which to choose. Ogg Vorbis for music and anything longer than a second: about a tenth of the size of a WAV, free of patents, decoded in Go everywhere. WAV for very short effects played often, where decoding costs more than the bytes. Both rewind when their source can seek, so a player can loop them: //go:embed waves.ogg var waves []byte stream, err := vorbis.Decode(bytes.NewReader(waves)) // a bytes.Reader seeks Not read yet. MP3 (its Go decoder, go-mp3, is archived) and Opus (Go decoders exist, but are young). A film's sound (AAC or Opus inside an MP4) will come from the system's own decoders, as its pictures do: see the design .

the-design.title: 🧭 The design
the-design.text: 🧭 The design A repository of its own Sound is its own package, depending on neither Go Renderer nor Go UI: A program without sound pays nothing. On Android, the output is C++ (Oboe) built with cgo; a program that plays nothing should not carry it. It is useful beyond a window. A tool with no window, or a game drawn with another engine, can play sound with it. It has its own life. An audio thread, suspending in the background, the phone's audio focus. The output: oto ebitengine/oto sends the sound to each system: it is what the Ebitengine game engine plays through, and it is kept up to date. System Through Android Oboe, which oto carries and links statically (nothing more goes in the package): AAudio from Android 11, OpenSL ES before, because AAudio did not always say when the sound moved from the speaker to headphones Linux PulseAudio, spoken in Go; ALSA when no PulseAudio runs, loaded when the program starts. No cgo macOS AudioToolbox Windows WASAPI A web page An AudioWorklet, started at the first touch or key, as browsers ask Nintendo 3DS The DSP, through libctru's ndsp, built with TinyGo: Go Sound mixes the players itself and hands the DSP buffers of 16-bit stereo frames Google advises Oboe or AAudio over OpenSL ES for new programs; Oboe makes that choice on each phone. Writing AAudio by hand (300 lines of C, as Go Renderer's films are) would cover Android alone and lose Oboe's fixes; miniaudio's Go binding (malgo) needs cgo everywhere and has no web output. Go Sound keeps oto behind two small interfaces ( output and voice ): the tests put a fake output there that pulls samples as the system would, and another output could take oto's place. How a sound plays A stream gives frames of samples, in its own rate and channels. The player converts them as they are read: channels to stereo, then frames to the context's rate, interpolating between neighbouring frames. A sound plays as long at any rate: its last frame is held for as long as it lasts. oto reads the player's frames from its own goroutine, mixes the players at their volumes and hands them to the system. The player counts the frames it gave. What is heard now is that count less what still waits in oto's and the system's buffers: Player.Position . Just after a loop starts again, what is heard is still the end of the time before. Films A film's pictures play today and its sound does not: Go Renderer's Android films decode their picture track only, and a browser's film is muted (browsers play no sound before a touch). The plan: Go Renderer decodes a film's sound track too, with a second of the phone's decoders ( MediaCodec ), and hands its samples out, playing nothing itself. Go UI 's window.Video gives those samples as a stream, and takes a clock: a small interface of its own, so Go UI need not know Go Sound. The sound leads. A picture can be dropped or shown twice and nobody notices; a gap in the sound is always heard. So a player's Position is the clock, and the film shows the picture due by then. In a browser the film's own element plays its sound, in step with its pictures; it is unmuted after the first touch. A small package joins the two where both are used (Go UI for Android, or a package here).

the-quest.title: The Go Sound quest
the-quest.text: The Go Sound quest Make a harbour you can hear, one level at a time. Each level teaches one piece of Go Sound and ends with a new sound. The quest map: a road from START through 6 levels — Tuner, Composer, Luthier, Recorder, Mixer and Sailor — to a final challenge, Harbour master We will build the sounds of a harbour : a beep, a tune, a foghorn made sample by sample, a file to keep it in, the sea and a bell mixed together, and an app with a button to sound the horn, which goes quiet when a phone puts it in the background. Every level has the same shape: the idea (explained with something from everyday life), the code , a checkpoint to know it works, and an optional bonus . Each level leaves you with a program that plays. Before you start You need Go 1.25 or later and speakers. Make a folder for the quest beside a copy of Go Sound: git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-sound mkdir harbour && cd harbour go mod init example.com/harbour go mod edit -require github.com/akrck02/go-sound@v0.0.0 -replace github.com/akrck02/go-sound=../go-sound Each level is a main.go (and sometimes a second file) in this folder. Run it with: go mod tidy # the first time go run . 🔇 No sound? Go Sound never stops your program for want of speakers: context.Err() says why it is silent. Every level prints it. On Linux you need PulseAudio, PipeWire or ALSA running; see Troubleshooting . The pictures of each checkpoint are the waves the code makes, drawn from its samples: what you should hear. Level 1 · The Tuner Mission Pieces Time Open the speakers and play a beep NewContext , NewPlayer , Tone 5 min The idea Think of a record player . The context is the amplifier and the speakers: a program has exactly one, and switches it on once. A player is a turntable on it, and the stream is the record it plays. You can have many turntables on one amplifier, playing at once. sound.Tone is the simplest record of all: one pure note. Build it package main import ( "log" "time" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ) func main() { context, err := sound.NewContext(sound.Options{Name: "Foghorn"}) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } <-context.Ready() // at once on a computer; after the first touch in a web page beep, err := context.NewPlayer(sound.Tone(440, 500*time.Millisecond, 0.5)) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } beep.Play() time.Sleep(time.Second) // the program must live while the sound plays if err := context.Err(); err != nil { log.Print("no sound: ", err) } } Play returns at once and the sound goes on by itself, so the program sleeps a second: if main returned, the sound would stop with it. Checkpoint You hear a clean A (440 vibrations a second) for half a second, with no click at its start or end: a tone rises and falls over a few milliseconds. Level 1: half a second of a steady wave, then silence Bonus (optional): higher, quieter Play an A one octave up (twice the frequency) at a quarter of the volume. Achievement unlocked: Tuner Learn more: Using Go Sound Level 2 · The Composer Mission Pieces Time Notes one after another IsPlaying , Close 5 min The idea A tune is a queue at a bakery : each note waits for the one before it to finish. A player tells you whether it is still playing with IsPlaying ; when it says no, the next note is served. Build it package main import ( "log" "time" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ) // note is a pitch and how long it lasts. type note struct { frequency float64 length time.Duration } func main() { context, err := sound.NewContext(sound.Options{Name: "Foghorn"}) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } <-context.Ready() tune := []note{{392, 300 * time.Millisecond}, {440, 300 * time.Millisecond}, {494, 300 * time.Millisecond}, {587, 600 * time.Millisecond}} for _, step := range tune { player, err := context.NewPlayer(sound.Tone(step.frequency, step.length, 0.4)) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } player.Play() for player.IsPlaying() { // wait for the note to end time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond) } player.Close() } } Close lets go of a player you will not use again. Checkpoint Four notes going up, G A B D , the last one longer. Level 2: four blocks of wave, the last twice as long Bonus (optional): a chord Play the first three notes at the same time instead. Achievement unlocked: Composer Level 3 · The Luthier Mission Pieces Time A foghorn, made sample by sample Stream , Format , Rewinder , SetLoop 10 min The idea A luthier makes instruments by hand. Here you make one in code: a stream is anything that can answer two questions — how is your sound written? ( Format ) and give me the next samples ( Read ). A sample is a number from −1 to 1: how far the speaker's cone is pushed at that instant. 48,000 of them make a second of sound. A foghorn is a low note with overtones (which make it rough), swelling in and fading out. Build it foghorn.go : package main import ( "io" "math" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ) // foghorn is a stream of its own: a low, rough note that swells and fades, as a foghorn does. type foghorn struct { rate int // frames a second frames int // how long it lasts, in frames position int // the next frame to read pitch float64 // its note, in hertz } func newFoghorn(rate int, seconds, pitch float64) *foghorn { return &foghorn{rate: rate, frames: int(seconds * float64(rate)), pitch: pitch} } // Format says the samples are mono, at the foghorn's rate: the context turns them into stereo. func (horn *foghorn) Format() sound.Format { return sound.Format{SampleRate: horn.rate, Channels: 1} } // Read writes as many frames as fit, and io.EOF once the horn has sounded. func (horn *foghorn) Read(samples []float32) (int, error) { written := 0 for written < len(samples) && horn.position < horn.frames { seconds := float64(horn.position) / float64(horn.rate) phase := 2 * math.Pi * horn.pitch * seconds // a fundamental and two overtones make it rough wave := math.Sin(phase) + 0.5*math.Sin(2*phase) + 0.25*math.Sin(3*phase) samples[written] = float32(0.3 * wave * horn.envelope(seconds)) written++ horn.position++ } if horn.position >= horn.frames { return written, io.EOF } return written, nil } // envelope is how loud the horn is at a moment: it swells over half a second and fades over one. func (horn *foghorn) envelope(seconds float64) float64 { length := float64(horn.frames) / float64(horn.rate) return math.Min(1, math.Min(seconds/0.5, (length-seconds)/1.0)) } // Rewind starts it again, so a player can loop it. func (horn *foghorn) Rewind() error { horn.position = 0 return nil } main.go : package main import ( "log" "time" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ) func main() { context, err := sound.NewContext(sound.Options{Name: "Foghorn"}) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } <-context.Ready() horn, err := context.NewPlayer(newFoghorn(context.SampleRate(), 3, 110)) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } horn.SetLoop(true) // over and over: it rewinds at its end horn.Play() time.Sleep(10 * time.Second) } The horn is mono (one channel) and the context plays stereo at its own rate: it converts the stream as it reads it, so a stream can be written in whatever format is simplest. Checkpoint A deep, buzzing horn that swells for half a second, holds, and fades, every three seconds. Level 3: a wave that grows over half a second, holds and fades over a second Bonus (optional): a sadder horn Make it a minor third lower, and slower to fade. Achievement unlocked: Luthier Learn more: Streams Level 4 · The Recorder Mission Pieces Time Keep the horn in a WAV file and play it back wav.Decode 8 min The idea A WAV file is a box of samples with a label on the lid: the label (the header ) says how fast and how many channels; the rest is the samples one after another. Programs ship their sounds as files and decode them back into streams. Build it Keep foghorn.go . Add wavfile.go , which writes any stream into a box: package main import ( "encoding/binary" "errors" "io" "math" "os" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ) // saveWAV writes a whole stream into a WAV file of 16-bit samples: a short header, then the // samples one after another. func saveWAV(path string, stream sound.Stream) error { format := stream.Format() var samples []int16 buffer := make([]float32, 4096*format.Channels) for { count, err := stream.Read(buffer) for _, sample := range buffer[:count] { samples = append(samples, int16(math.Max(-1, math.Min(1, float64(sample)))*32767)) } if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) { break } if err != nil { return err } } file, err := os.Create(path) if err != nil { return err } defer file.Close() dataSize := uint32(len(samples) * 2) header := []any{ [4]byte{'R', 'I', 'F', 'F'}, 36 + dataSize, [4]byte{'W', 'A', 'V', 'E'}, [4]byte{'f', 'm', 't', ' '}, uint32(16), uint16(1), uint16(format.Channels), uint32(format.SampleRate), uint32(format.SampleRate * format.Channels * 2), uint16(format.Channels * 2), uint16(16), [4]byte{'d', 'a', 't', 'a'}, dataSize, } for _, field := range header { if err := binary.Write(file, binary.LittleEndian, field); err != nil { return err } } return binary.Write(file, binary.LittleEndian, samples) } And main.go : package main import ( "bytes" "log" "os" "time" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" "github.com/akrck02/go-sound/wav" ) func main() { // keep the foghorn in a file, once if err := saveWAV("foghorn.wav", newFoghorn(22050, 3, 110)); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } // read it back, as a program reads the sounds it ships with file, err := os.ReadFile("foghorn.wav") if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } stream, err := wav.Decode(bytes.NewReader(file)) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } log.Printf("%d frames a second, %d channel(s)", stream.Format().SampleRate, stream.Format().Channels) context, err := sound.NewContext(sound.Options{Name: "Foghorn"}) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } <-context.Ready() player, err := context.NewPlayer(stream) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } player.SetVolume(0.5) player.Play() time.Sleep(4 * time.Second) } Checkpoint A file foghorn.wav of about 130 KB appears in the folder, the program prints 22050 frames a second, 1 channel(s) , and you hear the horn at half the volume. Open the file in any audio player: it is the same horn. Bonus (optional): ship it inside the program Programs for phones and web pages have no files beside them. Embed the WAV. Achievement unlocked: Recorder Learn more: Sound files Level 5 · The Mixer Mission Pieces Time The sea, a horn and a bell at the same time several players, SetVolume , Position 8 min The idea A mixing desk has a fader for each instrument. Each player is one: its own volume, its own start and stop, and the context adds them all into one sound for the speakers. The sea is noise, smoothed so it rumbles instead of hissing, rising and falling every six seconds. It never ends , so it needs no rewinding to loop. Build it Keep foghorn.go . Add sea.go : package main import ( "math" "math/rand/v2" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ) // sea is endless noise that rises and falls like waves: it never ends, so it needs no Rewind. type sea struct { rate int position int random *rand.Rand last float64 // the noise is smoothed, so it rumbles instead of hissing } func newSea(rate int) *sea { return &sea{rate: rate, random: rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2))} } func (water *sea) Format() sound.Format { return sound.Format{SampleRate: water.rate, Channels: 1} } func (water *sea) Read(samples []float32) (int, error) { for index := range samples { seconds := float64(water.position) / float64(water.rate) swell := 0.5 + 0.5*math.Sin(2*math.Pi*seconds/6) // a wave every six seconds water.last += 0.05 * (water.random.Float64()*2 - 1 - water.last) samples[index] = float32(water.last * swell * 2) water.position++ } return len(samples), nil } main.go : package main import ( "fmt" "log" "time" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ) func main() { context, err := sound.NewContext(sound.Options{Name: "Harbour"}) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } <-context.Ready() rate := context.SampleRate() waves, _ := context.NewPlayer(newSea(rate)) // three players: the context mixes them horn, _ := context.NewPlayer(newFoghorn(rate, 3, 110)) bell, _ := context.NewPlayer(sound.Tone(1320, 800*time.Millisecond, 0.3)) waves.SetVolume(0.6) waves.Play() for second := 0; second < 12; second++ { if second%6 == 0 { horn.Play() // a horn every six seconds; Play starts it again once it has ended } if second%4 == 2 { bell.Play() } fmt.Printf("%2d s horn at %v\n", second, horn.Position().Round(100*time.Millisecond)) time.Sleep(time.Second) } } Position tells how far into a sound what you hear now is: what was read, minus what still waits in the system's buffers. A film's pictures follow it to stay in time with its sound. Checkpoint Waves come and go; a horn sounds at 0 and 6 seconds, a bell at 2, 6 and 10. The terminal counts the seconds and the horn's position. Level 5: the sea swelling and ebbing, with the horn and the bell over it Bonus (optional): a storm Make the waves come twice as often and the sea louder, but keep the bell quiet. Achievement unlocked: Mixer Level 6 · The Sailor Mission Pieces Time A button to sound the horn, and quiet in the background Go UI, Suspend , Resume 8 min The idea A polite app is a sailor who stops whistling when he goes ashore : when the phone puts it in the background (another app, the screen locked), it goes quiet, and plays again when it comes back. Go UI's window tells you both moments: Options.Hidden and Options.Shown . Build it This level needs Go UI and Go Renderer beside Go Sound ( Go UI's Get started ): git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-renderer ../go-renderer git clone https://github.com/akrck02/go-ui ../go-ui go mod edit -require github.com/akrck02/go-ui@v0.0.0 -replace github.com/akrck02/go-ui=../go-ui go mod edit -require github.com/akrck02/go-renderer@v0.0.0 -replace github.com/akrck02/go-renderer=../go-renderer Keep foghorn.go , and replace main.go : package main import ( "flag" "log" "time" sound "github.com/akrck02/go-sound" ui "github.com/akrck02/go-ui" "github.com/akrck02/go-ui/window" ) func main() { options := window.Options{Title: "Foghorn"} options.RegisterFlags(flag.CommandLine) flag.Parse() context, err := sound.NewContext(sound.Options{Name: "Foghorn"}) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } horn, err := context.NewPlayer(newFoghorn(context.SampleRate(), 3, 110)) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } volume := float32(0.8) // on a phone: quiet in the background, and back when the app returns options.Hidden = func() { context.Suspend() } options.Shown = func() { context.Resume() } err = window.Run(options, func(screen *ui.Context) { screen.Box(ui.Layout{Direction: ui.Vertical, Padding: ui.Pad(24), Gap: 12, Width: ui.Grow()}, func() { screen.Heading("Foghorn") if screen.PrimaryIconButton("volume-2", "Sound the horn") { horn.Rewind() horn.Play() } screen.Label("Volume") if screen.Slider("volume", &volume, 0, 1) { horn.SetVolume(float64(volume)) } if horn.IsPlaying() { screen.Caption("Sounding…") screen.RequestFrame(100 * time.Millisecond) // look again soon: the sound ends on its own } if err := context.Err(); err != nil { screen.Caption("No sound: " + err.Error()) } }) }) if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } } The interface is drawn again only when something happens; while the horn sounds, RequestFrame asks to look again in a tenth of a second, so "Sounding…" goes away when it ends. Checkpoint A window with a button and a volume slider; the button sounds the horn. If there is no sound, the window says why under the slider. Level 6: Foghorn, a Sound the horn button and a volume slider; on this computer, with no speakers, the reason it is silent Bonus (optional): on your phone Package it for Android with Go UI for Android's tool and put the app in the background while the horn sounds: it stops, and plays on when you come back. Achievement unlocked: Sailor Learn more: On a phone Final challenge · Harbour master Put it all together in the app: the sea always playing quietly behind, the horn on its button, and a second button that rings the bell . A switch turns the sea on and off. Hint: three players made once, before window.Run . The sea loops with Play once and never ends; ui.Toggle edits a bool , and when it changes, Play or Pause the sea. Rare achievement unlocked: Harbour master Well done All seven achievements: Tuner, Composer, Luthier, Recorder, Mixer, Sailor and Harbour master You made sounds from nothing, kept them in files, mixed them and put them in an app. Ideas to keep going Idea Difficulty Hint A metronome ⭐ A short Tone played every time.Second * 60 / beats Seagulls ⭐⭐ A stream whose pitch slides up and down: change pitch inside Read Music from an Ogg file, looping ⭐⭐ vorbis.Decode of an embedded file, SetLoop(true) ( sound files ) Sounds for a Go UI for Android app ⭐⭐ Go UI for Android's gallery plays a note the same way A sound for a film ⭐⭐⭐ Not yet: see the roadmap Troubleshooting You see Why, and what to do no sound: oto: initialization failed: PulseAudio…; ALSA… No sound server or device: start PulseAudio or PipeWire, or plug in speakers. The program runs on, silent Lines starting ALSA lib … cannot find card '0' The same, said by ALSA itself; harmless The program ends before the sound main returned: Play does not wait. Sleep, or wait for IsPlaying sound: a program has one context; keep the first NewContext was called twice; make one and pass it around sound: the stream cannot start again Looping a stream with no Rewind ; give it one, or decode from a bytes.Reader Crackles Try Options{Latency: 100 * time.Millisecond} , or fewer players at once Silent in a web page Browsers allow sound only after the first touch or key: wait on context.Ready() ← All the documentation

using-go-sound.title: 🔊 Using Go Sound
using-go-sound.text: 🔊 Using Go Sound A context A program opens the speakers once, with a context. The system allows one per program; a second NewContext says ErrContextExists . context, err := sound.NewContext(sound.Options{Name: "Lighthouses"}) Option What it sets SampleRate How many frames a second are played: 48000 by default, the rate phones and most sound cards run at Latency How much sound is kept ready ahead of what is heard; 0 leaves it to the system. Shorter answers sooner, too short crackles Name The name a desktop's volume mixer shows NewContext returns at once. In a web page the browser lets sound start only after the person's first touch or key: context.Ready() is closed once it can. context.Err() tells what went wrong with the output (no sound device, a device unplugged). Players A player plays one stream. Make one for each sound that may play at the same time: the context mixes them. note, err := context.NewPlayer(sound.Tone(660, 600*time.Millisecond, 0.5)) note.Play() Call What it does Play , Pause , IsPlaying Plays from where it is (from the start once it has ended), stops there, and tells which SetVolume(volume) From 0, silent, to 1, as the sound was made SetLoop(true) Starts again at its end, for music and the sea; a stream that cannot start again says ErrNotRewindable Rewind Back to its start, dropping what was ready to be heard Position How far into the sound what is heard now is: what was read, less what still waits in the system's buffers Close Stops and lets go of it A stream of any sample rate and any number of channels plays: it is turned into stereo at the context's rate as it is read. A mono sound is heard on both sides, the first two channels of a surround one are kept, and other rates are resampled between neighbouring frames. Streams A stream gives frames of samples from -1 to 1. Decode a file with wav.Decode or vorbis.Decode ( sound files ), make a beep with sound.Tone , or write one: type Stream interface { Format() sound.Format // the sample rate and the channels Read(samples []float32) (int, error) // whole frames; io.EOF at the end } A stream that also has Rewind() error can loop. A decoder's stream rewinds when its source can seek: a file, or a bytes.Reader of an embedded file. On a phone A phone's applications go quiet when they leave the screen. Suspend the context then, and resume it when the program comes back. With Go UI: options.Hidden = func() { context.Suspend() } options.Shown = func() { context.Resume() } On Android the sound goes through Oboe, which oto carries: AAudio from Android 11, OpenSL ES before (AAudio did not always say when a phone switched from its speaker to headphones). Building for Android compiles that C++ with the NDK, so cgo needs both CC and CXX ; go-ui-apk sets both. On the Nintendo 3DS Built with TinyGo for the nintendo3ds target, a context plays through the console's DSP. oto does not reach the 3DS, so Go Sound mixes its players itself (the same mixer the tests try) and hands the DSP six buffers of a thirtieth of a second in turn: a fifth of a second ahead, so a few slow frames (a scene loading, a network handshake) pass without a crackle. The DSP needs its firmware , /3ds/dspfirm.cdc on the SD card, which homebrew tools dump from the console. Without it the context opens all the same and Err says why it is silent: show it, so the player knows. Yield once a frame. TinyGo's scheduler there is cooperative, and the buffers are filled from a goroutine: Go UI's window yields every frame; a loop of its own calls runtime.Gosched() . Choose the sounds' rate as the context's (22050 frames a second is plenty for the console's speakers): nothing is resampled, and the processor has less to mix. Ogg Vorbis music decodes as it plays, at full speed on a New 3DS; WAV suits short effects.
